title: Cairo
body: Cairo is where your house stands and where the sultan rules. Ibn Battuta said the city surged like the waves of the sea. Boats carry goods from here down the Nile to Alexandria and up the Nile to Qus.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 41 to 59; the sultan and the city, pp. 52 to 53
vol. 1, p. 71; the boat from Qus to Cairo in the flood, eight nights

title: Alexandria
body: Alexandria is Egypt's harbour on the Mediterranean Sea. Italian merchants came here to buy pepper and other goods. A merchant's handbook written about 1340 says goods brought into the port paid a duty of 20 in every hundred. Goods leaving paid nothing.

sources.at: Alexandria chapter, 1766 printing p. 58; the 1936 Evans page (p. 72) not seen
pp. 167 to 168; spices sold to European merchants at Alexandria

title: Famagusta
body: Famagusta is a port on the island of Cyprus. Venice forbade its merchants to trade in Egypt from 1323, and its galleys came back in 1345. Famagusta was a go-between for Venetian trade with Egypt, and it was one before the ban too.

sources.at: pp. 135 to 136; Famagusta as go-between, a role older than the ban on direct trade

title: Venice
body: Venice was a city of merchants on the Adriatic Sea. In 1323 it banned trade with Egypt, under pressure from the pope. In 1345 a new treaty with the sultan let its galleys sail to Alexandria again.

sources.at: pp. 135 to 137; the ban of 1323, the envoy of August 1344, the treaty and the galleys of 1345

title: Constantinople
body: Constantinople was the great city on the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean. A merchant's handbook of about 1340 lists flax from Alexandria among the goods sold there. The sea road from Alexandria is long, and the records say little about how Cairo houses used it.

sources.at: flax of Alexandria for sale at Constantinople and Pera; the page is approximate in the notes, about p. 123
estimate; no source read gives a sailing time or a Cairo house trading at Constantinople

title: Tunis
body: Tunis is a port on the coast of North Africa, west of Egypt by sea. In this game it is the far end of the sea road to the west. No record that was read says what Cairo houses sold there, so its prices are guesses.

sources.at: estimate; nothing was read on Tunis itself, and the leg from Alexandria is graded an estimate in the network notes

title: Qus
body: Qus is a town on the Nile in Upper Egypt. Goods from the Red Sea were loaded onto Nile boats here for Cairo and Alexandria. In 1326 Ibn Battuta went down the river from Qus to Cairo in eight nights, in the flood.

sources.at: p. 33; Qus as the Nile port for goods from the Red Sea
vol. 1, p. 69

title: Quseir
body: Quseir is a Red Sea port, five days by caravan from Qus. Some merchants liked it because the desert road was shorter. The sea trip north to it was harder, because a north wind blows over the Red Sea most of the year.

sources.at: p. 33; the shorter desert leg, the longer sea leg and the north wind for 80 percent of the year
vol. 2, p. 413 n. 3; five days from Qus

title: Aydhab
body: Aydhab is a port on the African shore of the Red Sea. Ibn Battuta wrote that one third of the city belonged to the sultan and two thirds to the king of the Beja. In 1326 (about June by Gibb's count) he found the crossing shut. The Beja king and the sultan's soldiers were at war, so he turned back.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 68 to 69; the one third and two thirds of the town, and the war of 1326

title: Jeddah
body: Jeddah is a port on the Arabian side of the Red Sea. Ships crossed to it from Aydhab. In 1332 Ibn Battuta did not board a ship at Jeddah that was bound for Quseir. It sank at sea, and about seventy pilgrims drowned.

sources.at: vol. 2, pp. 412 to 413 (the ship of 1332) and pp. 360 to 362 (a crossing)

title: Aden
body: Aden is a port at the southern mouth of the Red Sea. Ibn Battuta called it the port of the merchants of India. Merchants from India lived there, and so did merchants from Egypt.

sources.at: p. 149; the Karimi brought spices from Aden to Cairo, Alexandria and Damascus

title: Calicut
body: Calicut is a port on the Malabar coast of India, where pepper grows. Ibn Battuta wrote that men came there from China, Java, Ceylon, the Maldives, Yemen and Fars. A wrecked ship's cargo stayed with its owners there, and he said this made it a flourishing and busy city.

sources.at: vol. 4, pp. 812 and 815 to 816
no. 36, introduction; pepper bought on the Malabar coast, 1097 to 1098

title: Hormuz
body: Hormuz is a port at the mouth of the Persian Gulf. In these years the city stood on the island of Jarun. The old city, on the mainland, had been left behind soon after 1300.

sources.at: vol. 2, p. 400 nn. 117 to 118; New Hormuz founded on the island of Jarun shortly after 1300

title: Damascus
body: Damascus is a great city in Syria. In 1326 Ibn Battuta went there from Cairo in about 22 days, by Gibb's count from his dates. He wrote that the inns in the sands of Sinai had a watering-place and a shop.

title: Aleppo
body: Aleppo is a city in northern Syria. In this game it is the last Syrian stop before the long road east to Tabriz. The records that were read say little about its trade, so its prices are guesses.

sources.at: estimate; the leg from Damascus to Aleppo and on to Tabriz is graded an estimate in the network notes

title: Tabriz
body: Tabriz is a city in Persia on the road east. After the Mongol ruler Abu Said died in late 1335, rival rulers took parts of his lands. In 1340 the ruler of Tabriz seized the goods of many Genoese merchants, and Genoa banned trade with Tabriz.

sources.at: vol. 2, pp. 339 to 341 and note 234; Tabriz among the cities taken by claimants
ch. 4, the Genoese ban of Tabriz; Lopez 1943, pp. 183 to 184, is the page Greif cites for the paragraph

title: Samarkand
body: Samarkand is a city in Central Asia, at the far end of the land road east. Raw silk came to Egypt from Iran, Central Asia and China. A house can send an agent that far, but it is a long and risky road.

sources.at: pp. 168 to 172; raw silk from Iran, Central Asia and China
estimate; the leg from Tabriz is graded an estimate, and no Cairo house at Samarkand was found

title: Tuat
body: Tuat is a group of oases in the Sahara. In this game it is the desert stop where a Cairo agent meets the caravans. This is a simple map: no record that was read shows a Cairo house sending its own agents to Tuat.

sources.at: vol. 4, p. 975 n. 102; his return from Takedda by way of Tuat took from 12 September to about December 1353
estimate; the reach of the roads rests on few sources

title: Walata
body: Walata is a town on the south side of the Sahara. Ibn Battuta reached it in 1352, two full months after leaving Sijilmasa. At Taghaza he was told that a load of salt sold at Walata for eight to ten mithqals.

sources.at: vol. 4, p. 947 for the salt price, told to him at Taghaza, and p. 950 for the two months

title: Gao
body: Gao is a town on the Niger river in West Africa. Ibn Battuta did not go from Walata straight to Gao. He reached the Niger towns by way of Mali.

sources.at: vol. 4, pp. 969 to 971

title: The Nile
body: The Nile runs through Egypt and carries boats between Cairo, Alexandria and Qus. It floods in late summer and early autumn, after the June monsoon rains on the highlands of Ethiopia. Ibn Battuta saw the flood in July 1326.

sources.at: p. 125 and the section on the flood; the monsoon rains on the Ethiopian highlands
vol. 1, p. 69; the flood season of 1326

title: The Red Sea
body: The Red Sea is a long, narrow sea between Egypt and Arabia. A north wind blows over it for most of the year, so ships going north have a hard time. Goods from India came up it, crossed the desert to Qus, and went down the Nile.

sources.at: p. 33; the north wind for 80 percent of the year, and the route to Qus
vol. 2, p. 372; Aden as the port of the merchants of India

title: The Sahara
body: The Sahara is the great desert south and west of Egypt. At Taghaza, Ibn Battuta saw houses built of blocks of salt and roofed with camel skins. He wrote that beyond it lay ten days' travel with no water, or only rarely. He himself found rain pools.

sources.at: vol. 4, p. 946 for Taghaza on day 25, and p. 947 for the ten days without water

title: The monsoon coast
body: The monsoon coast is the western shore of India. Ships from Arabia sailed there. Calicut was one of its chief ports.

sources.at: monsoon timing and the Red Sea trade, as the notes describe the book
dhows and the monsoons; the book was not paged in the notes

title: Mansa Musa
body: Mansa Musa was the king of Mali. He passed through Cairo in the summer of 1324 on his way to Mecca, with a very large company. Al-Umari wrote that the Cairenes made great profits from the Malians and that the price of gold fell.

sources.at: summer 1324; the departure on 14 October 1324

title: Ibn Battuta
body: Ibn Battuta was a scholar from Tangier who travelled for about thirty years. He landed at Alexandria in April 1326 and went on to Cairo. He told his story long afterward. His account of Egypt is put together from several visits.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 18; Alexandria on 5 April 1326, and the editor note on the several visits, p. 32 n.

title: al-Nasir Muhammad
body: Al-Nasir Muhammad ruled Egypt and Syria as sultan for most of the years from 1293 until he died in June 1341. Ibn Battuta called him a man of generous character. After he died, eight of his sons ruled one after another. The amirs, his chief officers, chose who sat on the throne.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 52 to 53, and the editor note on the sultan reign
pp. 53 and 74 to 76

title: al-Umari
body: Al-Umari was a writer who came to live in Egypt and wrote about 1337 to 1338. He did not see Mansa Musa's visit. He wrote what the Cairenes told him, including the claim that gold stayed cheap for about twelve years, which only he says.

sources.at: doubts the long effect; the article was read only in summary

title: al-Maqrizi
body: Al-Maqrizi was a historian of Cairo who lived from 1364 to 1442. He also served as a muhtasib, the officer who watched the markets. He wrote seventy years or more after these events, so many of his stories are what earlier writers told him.

sources.at: p. 217 n. 46; his dates

title: Karimi merchants
body: The Karimi were great merchants who brought spices from Aden to Cairo, Alexandria and Damascus. They included families such as the Ibn al-Kuwayk. Historians do not agree on how tightly they were organised, and Sato calls them a loose group.

title: Venetians
body: The Venetians were merchants from Venice who bought spices at Alexandria. Their state sent convoys of galleys there each year from 1301. The convoys stopped after 1312 and began again in 1345. In 1323 Venice banned trade with Egypt, though some trade went on.

sources.at: pp. 117 and 135 to 137

title: Genoese
body: The Genoese were merchants from Genoa. Genoese clerks had written contracts in Cyprus and Cilicia for trade to Egypt since at least 1274. A historian of the popes finds no sign that the Genoese stopped trading with Egypt in the years Venice's trade was hampered.

sources.at: p. 125; Genoese notary contracts of 1274 and 1302

title: Beja
body: The Beja lived around Aydhab, on the African shore of the Red Sea. Ibn Battuta wrote that their king held two thirds of the city and the sultan one third. In 1326 the Beja king was at war with the sultan's soldiers, and the crossing from Aydhab was closed.

sources.at: vol. 1, pp. 68 to 69

title: Pepper
body: Pepper grew on the Malabar coast of southern India. The Karimi brought it by sea and desert to Cairo, and Italians bought it at Alexandria. It was packed in a basket called a sporta. A sporta of pepper held 5 cantars, a heavy weight, and the game counts it as about one load.

sources.at: no. 36, introduction; pepper on the Malabar coast
1766 printing p. 58; a sporta of pepper is 5 cantars; the 1936 Evans page (p. 71) not seen

title: Silk
body: Silk was woven in Alexandria and Cairo, and raw silk came from Iran, Central Asia and China. In 1326 the sultan owned a silk inn in Alexandria. Linen was the usual cloth in Egypt, so silk stood out.

sources.at: pp. 168 to 172 and p. 180
the sultan property list of 16 April 1326

title: Gold
body: Gold dust came to Egypt from West Africa by the Sahara roads. The mint at Cairo turned it into dinars. In 1335 the sultan's officer ordered merchants and goldsmiths to bring their gold to the mint, because coin was short. The game counts gold by the chest, not by the load.

sources.at: p. 135; the coin shortage of 1335

title: Salt
body: Salt was cut at Taghaza in the Sahara in thick slabs, and a camel carried two. At Taghaza Ibn Battuta was told what salt sold for. A load fetched eight to ten mithqals at Walata. In Mali it fetched twenty to thirty, sometimes forty. In this game salt is bought and sold only on the Sahara road.

title: Porcelain
body: Porcelain was made in China. Ibn Battuta saw it there and wrote that it cost no more than ordinary pots cost at home. The game's porcelain is pale green celadon, and nothing that was read gives its price in Cairo.

sources.at: the China passage, pp. 282 to 283

title: Glass
body: Glass was made in Egypt. In 1326 the sultan's property in Alexandria included a glass-works that had once been a soap-works. Venice wanted ash from Egypt and Syria to make its own glass, so your house sells glass and does not buy it.

sources.at: the property list of 16 April 1326
p. 111; Venice wanting ash for its glass

title: Linen
body: Linen cloth and flax were Egyptian goods. A merchant's handbook of about 1340 lists flax from Alexandria for sale in Constantinople. Linen cloth was sold by the arm's length.

sources.at: print p. 72 for cloth by the braccia; flax at Constantinople, about p. 123

title: Sugar
body: Sugar cane was grown on a large scale in Upper Egypt by the 1300s. It was shipped as pointed loaves. At Ramadan in 1344 to 1345 the sultan gave his officers three times as much sugar as under al-Nasir Muhammad. Al-Maqrizi put its worth at 30,000 dinars.

sources.at: pp. 91 to 99 and pp. 104 to 105
print pp. 362 to 363; the loaf with a point

title: Incense
body: Incense is a resin that is burned for its smell. A merchant's handbook of about 1340 says good incense is thick, white and clean. Yellow lumps are old or badly kept. It was sold at Alexandria by weight and packed in cases.

sources.at: print p. 69 for the sale list; the note on quality about p. 368

title: Copper
body: Italian merchants brought copper to Egypt in the 1300s from the north shore of Anatolia. It was weighed at Alexandria. No price for copper in these years was found, so the game's prices are guesses.

sources.at: about p. 50 (page not confirmed) and p. 47 n. 42
print p. 70; copper under the cantar gerui

title: Wool cloth
body: Wool cloth came from Europe and was sold by the piece. In 1340 a handbook lists it for sale at Alexandria, with the duty of 20 in every hundred. It was a small import then, and it became a large one in the 1400s.

sources.at: print p. 72
about p. 171, quoting Ashtor

title: Qirad
body: A qirad was a partnership. One partner put up the money or goods, and the other travelled and did the work. In the contracts Goitein read, the traveller took a smaller share of the profit, usually one third. He did not share in a loss of money.

sources.at: the rules of the qirad from the law books

title: Monsoon
body: A monsoon is a wind that blows one way for months and then turns and blows the other way. The June monsoon rains on the highlands of Ethiopia also made the Nile flood.

sources.at: monsoon timing and the Red Sea trade
dhows and the monsoons
the Nile flood and the monsoon rains

title: Caravan
body: A caravan was a group of travellers and pack animals that went together, so they could share water and guard each other. In 1326 Ibn Battuta crossed the desert from Edfu to Aydhab in 15 days. He hired camels and went with a party of Arabs. He went from Cairo to Damascus in about three weeks, by Gibb's count.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 67 for Edfu to Aydhab; p. 118 n. 182 for Cairo to Damascus, counted by Gibb from the dates

title: Caravanserai
body: A caravanserai was an inn for travellers and their animals and goods. In Egypt such buildings had several names, such as khan, funduq and wikala. On the road to Damascus, Ibn Battuta wrote, the khans in the sands of Sinai had a watering-place. Each had a shop outside.

sources.at: Background n. 17; khan, funduq and wikala as one kind of building
vol. 1, pp. 71 to 72

title: Broker
body: A broker was a go-between. He helped a seller and a buyer agree on a deal, and he was paid for it. A merchant who knew a good broker could find buyers faster in a strange market.

sources.at: definition of the word only; the letters show how merchants and their agents worked, and no period claim is made here

title: Muhtasib
body: The muhtasib was the officer who watched over the markets. In 1341 Cairo's muhtasib found a seller keeping a store of spoiled birds, and the seller was reprimanded and punished in public. Al-Maqrizi, the historian, held this post himself.

sources.at: section 1, n. 95; the finding of 1341

title: Dinar
body: The dinar was a gold coin, and in this game it is your money. Coins were weighed rather than counted, because real coins varied a little. In the account books, one dinar counted as 20 dirhams. A mithqal is the weight of one dinar.

sources.at: pp. 121 to 123; the dinar, the dirham and the account rate of 20

title: Dirham
body: The dirham was a silver coin, and only about two thirds to three quarters of it was silver. In the account books 20 dirhams made a dinar. In the market in the 1320s and 1330s, 22 to 25 dirhams bought a dinar of gold.

sources.at: print p. 72; 23 to 25 dirhams to the bezant
pp. 269 to 273; 25 and 22 dirhams to the mithqal

title: Load
body: A load is the amount a camel could carry, and this game counts most goods in loads. A basket of pepper called a sporta held 5 cantars, a heavy weight, and the game counts it as about one load. Gold is different. It is counted by the chest, because it is worth so much for its weight.

sources.at: 1766 printing p. 58; the sporta; the 1936 Evans page (p. 71) not seen
p. 98; himl, the Arabic word for a load

title: Toll
body: A toll is a fee paid to pass a gate, a road or a port. At Aydhab the town was shared between the sultan and the Beja king. Every toll you pay comes out of your profit.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 68; the one third and two thirds of the town

title: Customs
body: Customs are taxes on goods that come into a port or leave it. A handbook of about 1340 says goods brought into Alexandria paid 20 in every hundred, and goods leaving paid nothing. Gold and silver paid less: 4 and 3.5 in every hundred, and 2 after the treaty of 1345.

sources.at: print p. 72

title: Factor
body: A factor was an agent who did business for a merchant in another town. He bought, sold and kept accounts, and the merchant's letters and goods passed through his hands. Your agents on the roads do this work for your house.

sources.at: definition of the word only; the letters show how merchants and agents worked, and no period claim is made here

title: Geniza
body: The Geniza is a huge store of old letters and contracts found in Cairo. Many were written by Jewish merchants and their agents. Most are from about 950 to 1250, so they show how trade worked and not what happened in the 1330s.

sources.at: letters mostly 950 to 1250
Geniza merchant letters and contracts

title: Pilgrimage
body: A pilgrimage is a journey to a holy place. Muslims are asked to make the pilgrimage to Mecca, called the Hajj, once in a lifetime if they can. Caravans left Cairo for it every year, and merchants went along. Mansa Musa came to Egypt on this journey.

sources.at: vol. 1, p. 59; he went up the Nile with the pilgrim caravan in May 1326

title: Ramadan
body: Ramadan is the month of fasting for Muslims, who eat and drink nothing between dawn and sunset. It is also a month of prayer and giving. The sultan gave sugar to his officers at Ramadan.

sources.at: pp. 104 to 105; the Ramadan sugar grant

title: Dhow and galley
body: A dhow is a sailing ship of the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea. A galley is a long ship with oars and sails that crossed the Mediterranean. Ships went where the wind and the season let them.

sources.at: dhows and the monsoons
the Venice galley convoys

title: How agents were paid
body: A traveller did not get a wage the way a clerk does. His living costs, and the costs of carrying the goods and paying customs, were often paid out of the shared money. Or he kept a share of the profit, usually one third. Or he was paid a commission, a fee for one special job. A man who ran a shop for partners often got a small sum each week as well as his share.

sources.at: p. 316; the commission paid for a special service
p. 317; the worker's share, normally one third
pp. 325 to 326; the traveller's costs paid out of the partnership, and the small weekly sums of a man sitting in the store

title: Orders
body: When a merchant sent an agent away, the terms were written down. They said where the agent could trade and what he could do. In this game that page is your orders, or your paper of orders. An agent who went beyond them and lost money paid the whole loss himself. A page of orders cannot say everything, so an agent often had to use his own judgement.

sources.at: p. 327; a manager who broke the conditions of the contract
